rv.q: The rhetorical move is effective, like pulling a tablecloth from a fully set table, but it’s also familiar.
But the show can't quite shake the feel of an entertaining lecture.
This riveting, shocking show traces human milestones over the last 75,000 years leading up to the Canberra, New South Wales fires of 2019-2020, the worst in human history.
But I mean no disparagement when I say that “Deep History” works best as a lecture about climate change – one that is extremely well-timed...
While it lasts, David Finnigan’s Deep History offers some cool aperçus on one of the most pressing issues of our times.

Deep History is an assemblage of selective scientific fact, historical speculation, personal stories and seemingly spontaneous drama that suggests how even the most concerned people still are not ready to deal with the climate crisis.
But Deep History is closer to a TED Talk than theatrical art.
Deep History truly begins to shine as Finnigan’s experiment unravels and the actual lessons from who we were and how we got here are uncovered.
It's a powerful engaging theatrical presentation, bordering on the idea of required viewing.
This is a different type of theatre worth investigating and you will be welcomed by a warm and genial host.
He has at least proved one point: that art on the climate crisis can be both grippingly entertaining and thought-provoking.
His show is an engaging but sometimes awkward blend of personal history, documentary (complete with slides and video footage), and science lesson.
It was the mechanism of how he did it as abrupt pieces of interruptions that didn’t flow together into a cohesive whole.
It certainly can’t hurt, as Finnigan ably demonstrates.

cn.t: Critics find Finnigan's climate change solo show informative and timely, though many question whether it's more TED talk than theater. Praised for its engaging storytelling and urgency, but faulted for lacking theatrical depth.

vr.q: It's informative with valuable insights about the climate crisis, but in the end it was too self-reflective to really say something or leave a message that sticks.
